title: L6 review: how Spark runs a query, and why it might be slow
text:
How Spark runs our query

Where does each step of the query run?
The lecture’s example data are the New York City yellow taxi trips from 2011 to 2013, about 520 million trips in 36 monthly Parquet files on S3. An EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge, runs the query from L5: the rides and the average total per payment type for June 2012. Each core node runs one executor with 4 cores, so the cluster has 8 slots.
by_pay = (spark.read.parquet("s3://…/taxi/parquet/")
  .filter((F.col("tpep_pickup_datetime") >= "2012-06-01")
        & (F.col("tpep_pickup_datetime") <  "2012-07-01"))
  .groupBy("payment_type")
  .agg(F.count("*").alias("rides"),
       F.avg("total_amount").alias("avg_total")))
by_pay.collect()

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each step of the June 2012 query, where does it run? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- read the trip rows from the files: `spark.read.parquet` / `FROM` :: a task, on its own partition
    > Each task fetches the byte ranges of its own Spark partition.
- keep only the trips for June 2012: `filter` / `WHERE` :: a task, on its own partition
    > The filter keeps or drops each row without looking at any other partition.
- drop the columns no longer needed (Spark adds this step itself) :: a task, on its own partition
    > The driver adds this step to the plan; each task does it, reading only the columns needed.
- finish the count and average per payment type: `groupBy().agg()` / `GROUP BY` :: a task, after the Exchange
    > A task can total its own rows, but a payment type's rows sit in several partitions, so the partial totals cross an Exchange first. "The driver" is wrong here: it never adds up trip rows.
- return the answer to your program: `collect()` :: the driver
    > `collect()` hands the 5 final rows to the driver, the process that runs your program.
- :: YARN, on the primary node
    > This reads the cluster manager as doing the work. YARN only hands each executor its memory and cores on a core node; the query's steps run in those executors, and the driver plans them.

section: From code to a physical plan
text:
From code to a physical plan

Self-check: what does an Exchange do?
In the measured run of the June 2012 query on the 2 core nodes, stage 1 reads the 36 monthly files and computes partial totals, and stage 2 finishes the count and average per payment type. Between them is an Exchange (shuffle). This is what happened around it:
stage 1, scan       52 tasks on core nodes 1 and 2; 1 task, on node 1, had June 2012 trips
partial rows        5 from that task, one per payment type, 367 B in all
stage 2, planned    1000 shuffle partitions (EMR's default)
stage 2, ran        1 task, on core node 2: adaptive execution merged the 1000 into 1
result              5 rows, to the driver

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## In the June 2012 run, what moves over the network in the `Exchange` (shuffle)?

1. [ ] Input files, read again from S3
    > This treats the `Exchange` as a second scan. Stage 2 reads what stage 1 wrote, here 5 partial rows; the input files are read once, by stage 1.
1. [ ] Every June 2012 trip the scan kept
    > This skips the partial totals. Stage 1 already added up its June 2012 trips into one row per payment type, so only those 5 rows go into the `Exchange`.
1. [x] Rows for a task on another node
    > The task on node 1 wrote 5 rows for the stage-2 task on node 2, so those 367 B went over the network. Had the stage-2 task run on node 1, those rows would not have crossed the network.

## In the June 2012 run, when could the stage-2 task start?

1. [ ] As soon as the task with the June 2012 trips had written its 5 rows
    > This starts stage 2 on the only rows that exist. Spark cannot know that the other 51 tasks will add nothing until they finish, so every task of stage 1 must end first.
1. [x] Once the last of the 52 stage-1 tasks had finished
    > Stage 2 needs the partial rows from all of stage 1, which is what makes the `Exchange` a stage boundary: the one stage-2 task started once the last scan task had finished, although only one of the 52 had rows for it.
1. [ ] As soon as the driver had built the plan
    > This option confuses building the plan with producing data. The driver builds the plan before tasks run, but stage 2 must wait until the stage-1 tasks produce their rows.

## Spark planned 1000 shuffle partitions for stage 2 of the June 2012 query. What decides which of them gets a row?

1. [ ] Node that wrote the row
    > This expects rows to stay where they were written. A row can go to a task on any node; here the rows from node 1 went to a task on node 2.
1. [x] Row's key, its payment type
    > All rows with the same payment type go to the same shuffle partition. The plan's `hashpartitioning(payment_type, …)` hashes the key to choose that partition, so one task can finish the payment type's totals.
1. [ ] Order in which rows were read
    > This option assigns rows by read order, which would split one payment type across several tasks. Rows with the same key must go to the same shuffle partition regardless of read order.

section: Running the plan: stages, tasks and waves
text:
Running the plan: stages, tasks and waves

Which part of the run explains the wait?
The rides and average total per payment type for June 2012 ran over the 36 monthly files of taxi trips, about 520 million trips, on an EMR cluster with 2 core nodes (8 slots). The parts of the run, in order:








Part of the run
What happened
Time




Stage 1, scan: read, keep the June 2012 trips, partial totals
52 tasks, 36 of them read rows; a typical task took 1.65 s (9 in 10 took 1.75 s or less)
8.58 s


Exchange: partial rows to stage 2
5 rows, 367 B, written by 1 task; stage 2 waited 0 ms to fetch them (9 in 10 runs: 1 ms or less)
none of its own: writing is in stage 1, fetching in stage 2


Stage 2, group totals
1 task
0.011 s


Whole query

8.90 s



Each time is the median over 50 runs of the query (5 runs on each of 10 clusters).

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A teammate wants to shorten the June 2012 query and starts with the group-by, because it is the one step that needs rows from other nodes. Which part of the run should a change target first?

1. [ ] Stage 2: group totals
    > This expects the group-by to be the heavy step. Stage 2 ran one task for 0.011 s, because it added up only 5 partial rows.
1. [ ] `Exchange` between the stages
    > This expects moving data between nodes to cost most. 5 rows, 367 B, went into it, and stage 2 waited 0 ms to fetch them.
1. [x] Stage 1: scan
    > 8.58 s of the 8.90 s query, against 0.011 s for stage 2: reading the 36 files is the cost. The field that shows it is the stage's *Duration*.

Slide: 22 (also 19)


What sets the time of stage 1?
Stage 1 of the June 2012 query reads the 36 monthly files of taxi trips, keeps the June 2012 trips and computes partial totals. It runs on 2 core nodes, each with one executor of 4 cores; one executor core, a slot, runs one task at a time. Spark cut the files into 52 input partitions, one task each:
tasks that read rows     36, about 1.65 s each (9 in 10 at 1.75 s or less)
tasks that read nothing  16, a few milliseconds each
slots                    2 executors × 4 cores = 8
stage time               8.58 s
The tasks that run at the same time, one per slot, form a wave (a term from Hadoop). The Spark UI does not name it, but its event timeline shows each wave as a column of task bars.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Each slot runs one task at a time. What sets how long stage 1 takes on the 8 slots?

1. [ ] Total work split evenly over 8 slots
    > This calculation assumes the work can be divided evenly: 36 × 1.65 s ÷ 8 is about 7.4 s. Each task runs as a whole in one slot, so the 36 tasks cannot be spread evenly over 8 slots.
1. [ ] Slowest single task
    > This applies when one task is much slower than the rest. Here the reading tasks take about the same time, 1.65 s, and the stage takes 8.58 s, about five of them back to back.
1. [x] Number of waves of tasks
    > The 36 tasks that read rows fill 4 waves of 8 and a fifth wave of 4, while the other 4 slots run the 16 empty tasks and then wait: 5 waves of about 1.65 s is about 8.25 s, close to the 8.58 s measured. The 16 tasks that read nothing add only milliseconds.

text:
What can make queries slow

Rows or totals into the Exchange?
From here on the lecture uses only the June 2012 trips, 15,096,468 of them (15.1 M), and steps run on 2 core nodes (8 slots):
trips       the June 2012 trips: 1 Parquet file, 8 row groups, read by 8 tasks; not bucketed
zones       the 265-row taxi zone table, a CSV file
broadcast   Spark automatically copies a table to every executor when it estimates
            the table at 10 MiB or less

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each step on the June 2012 trips, what goes into an `Exchange` (shuffle)? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- count and average per payment type: `groupBy().agg()` :: partial totals
    > Each of the 8 reading tasks sends one row containing a count and a sum for each payment type it saw. That produces 40 rows for the 15.1 M trips.
- number of trips per pickup day: `groupBy().count()` :: partial totals
    > A count is a sum of ones: each task counts its own rows per day and sends one count per day it saw. The final stage adds those counts, so only a few rows per task cross the `Exchange`.
- each trip gets its payment type's average next to it: a window query :: every row
    > The average goes onto every trip of that payment type, so no task can add its rows up first: all 15,096,468 trips, 86.5 MB, went into the `Exchange`.
- join the trips to another large table, over 10 MiB :: every row
    > Neither table is small enough for Spark to copy, so both tables send their rows into an `Exchange` by the join key. The trips joined to the zone table with broadcast turned off sent all 15.1 M trips, 88 MB.
- join the trips to the 265-row zone table: `F.broadcast(zones)` :: no shuffle `Exchange`
    > The plan uses a `BroadcastExchange` to copy the 265-row table to every executor, while the shuffle `Exchange` named in the answer would repartition the trips by key. The trips remain in their Spark partitions, where each task matches its rows against the copied table.
- keep only the trips for the first week of June 2012 and calculate two new columns from values in each row :: no shuffle `Exchange`
    > This is a narrow step because each task keeps its rows and computes the columns within its own Spark partition, without moving data between Spark partitions.
- :: one average per task
    > With one average per payment type from each task, the final stage could only average the averages, which is wrong when the tasks hold different numbers of trips (L5). A task sends a count and a sum instead, which the final stage adds up and divides.

title: L6 review: how Spark runs a query, and why it might be slow
text:
Checks for a slow stage

Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?
A later query joins the June 2012 trips to the 5-row payment-type names table, a CSV file, with Spark’s automatic broadcast turned off. It runs on 2 core nodes (8 slots) and takes 1.65 s. The Spark UI’s stage page shows this for the stage after the Exchange (shuffle):
tasks             3; adaptive execution merged payment types 4 and 5 into the other two
records           7.8 million in one task, the trips paid by cash; 7.2 million in one, paid by card;
                  about 36,000 in the third, payment type 3
other slots       idle while the two large tasks run

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Cash and card are hot keys because each key sends millions of rows to one task. Which change shortens this stage the most?

1. [x] Broadcast the names table
    > Copying the names table to every executor keeps the trips out of the `Exchange` and in their Spark partitions, so each task joins its own rows. On the same cluster, this reduced the measured time from 1.65 s to 0.71 s; case P2.2 recommends broadcast before adaptive execution and reserves salting for last.
1. [ ] Give each task more memory
    > This treats the long tasks as spills. More memory moves no rows: the cash trips still land in one task, and that task still processes all 7.8 million of them.
1. [ ] Run the join on the salted copy of the trips (a copy with an extra value that splits each payment type among several files in its folder partition)
    > This layout lets more tasks share the scan, while the join still routes every cash row to one task by payment type. The salt can split the join only when both sides include it in the join key (case P2.2).

Another query sorts the June 2012 trips by pickup time, on the same cluster but with each executor given 1 GiB of memory. A spill occurs when a task runs short of memory and writes intermediate data to disk. The stage after the Exchange shows this:
shuffle partitions  8, set with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
tasks             8
task duration     median 2.4 s, longest 2.6 s
records           about 1.9 million in every task
Spill (disk)      about 150 MB in every task
GC time           about 0.8 s in every task

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Every task spilled, and the tasks are of even size, so the cause is memory per task. Which change helps?

1. [ ] Fewer shuffle partitions, so fewer tasks compete for memory
    > Fewer shuffle partitions put more rows in each task, which increases the memory needed by each task.
1. [ ] Write the input with more row groups
    > This applies the scan fix to the wrong stage. Row groups divide the reading tasks; the rows per task after the `Exchange` are set by the number of shuffle partitions.
1. [x] More shuffle partitions, so each task holds fewer rows
    > More shuffle partitions reduce the rows per task after the `Exchange`. With 16 shuffle partitions, the stage runs 16 tasks of about 0.95 million rows, each needing half as much memory; giving each task more memory also works (Problem 4).

title: L6 review: how Spark runs a query, and why it might be slow
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise them in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Spark: shuffles and slow stages
Narrow transformation. A step each task does on its own partition, so no rows move between partitions: filter, select, withColumn.
Wide transformation. A step that needs rows from other partitions, such as groupBy, orderBy, a window or most joins. Spark adds a shuffle before it.
Shuffle (Exchange). Moving rows between partitions for the next stage: each task writes its rows to its node’s disk, and the next stage’s tasks read them, often from other nodes.
Window query. A step that computes a value over a group of rows and puts it on each row, such as each trip’s payment-type average next to the trip. Every row goes into an Exchange.
Hot key. One join, window or sort value with far more rows than the others. All its rows go to one task, which runs long after the rest of its stage; more nodes do not help.
Spill. Writing to the node’s disk when the rows a task sorts, groups or shuffles do not fit in its share of executor memory. The result is correct but slower.


Spark: how a job runs
Driver. The program that coordinates a Spark application: it runs your code, builds the query plan and sends tasks to the executors.
Executor. A Spark program running on an EMR core or task node. It runs tasks and keeps their data in its memory or on the node’s disk.
Partition. A chunk of rows that one task processes as one unit. When reading files it holds one or more splits, each a byte range of one file, planned from the file sizes and the number of slots.
Task. One stage’s work on one chunk of rows, run in one slot: by default, one executor core.
Slot. One executor core, as room to run one task on one Spark partition at a time. An executor with 4 cores runs 4 tasks at once; our EMR nodes have one per vCPU.
Stage. A set of tasks Spark can run before rows have to move between partitions. Every task in it runs the same steps on a different partition.
Wave. The set of a stage’s tasks that run at the same time, one per slot. 36 reading tasks on 8 slots need 5 of them.
Transformation. A step such as filter or groupBy(...).count() that is only recorded in the plan. No task runs until an action asks for a result.
Action. On a Spark DataFrame, a call such as df.count(), df.collect() or df.write.parquet() that makes Spark run the plan built so far. Unlike pandas, where each step runs as soon as you call it.


EMR cluster
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node. The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node. An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node. An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing data.


Also used on this page
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Row group. A horizontal block inside one Parquet file, holding one column chunk per column. Its size is set when the file is written, and a file can hold one or many.
Folder partition. A dataset layout with one named location per value of a column, such as day=2012-06-14/ (on S3, a prefix). A filter on that column skips the other locations without opening them.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.

section: How Spark divides and coordinates the work
text:
How Spark divides and coordinates the work

What does Spark run again when a core node is lost?
A Spark query over a year of lift-gate scans in S3 runs on an EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge. Each core node has an executor, a process that runs 4 tasks at a time (8 slots in total). The query’s scan stage has 36 tasks, each reading one piece of the input. This is the snapshot of what the cluster had run before the failure:
scan stage, 36 tasks      finished   running   not started
core node 1                  10         4
core node 2                  10         4
total                        20         8           8
Then core node 2 fails, taking its executor and its disk with it.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## After the core node 2 failure, besides the 8 tasks that have not started, how many scan tasks does Spark run again?

1. [x] 14
    > When core node 2 was lost, its 4 running tasks stopped and the output of its 10 finished tasks went with the node. Spark reruns those 14 tasks from their pieces in S3, while the output of core node 1's finished tasks is still there.
1. [ ] 4
    > This treats a finished task as safe. A finished scan task's output waits on its own node for the next stage; when that node is lost, that output is lost too, and the task that wrote it reruns.
1. [ ] 36
    > This applies the single-process rule from L4, where a failed DuckDB process restarts the whole query. Spark can reread the input pieces from S3, so it reruns only the tasks whose work was lost.
1. [ ] 28
    > Core node 1 is still there, with its executor and its disk, so its 10 finished tasks keep their output and its 4 running tasks carry on. Only core node 2's work is lost.

Slide: 10 (also 8)

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Amazon EMR

How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?
An EMR cluster has three kinds of nodes, all m7g.xlarge with 4 vCPUs each, at $0.2227 an hour per node:
primary   1 node
core      4 nodes
task      3 nodes
A node runs at most one executor, which gets 4 cores, one per vCPU of the node, and so runs 4 tasks at a time (4 slots).

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?

1. [x] 28
    > The 4 core nodes and 3 task nodes run executors, so 7 × 4 = 28 tasks run at once. The primary node manages the cluster and runs no executor. You pay for 8 nodes, about \$1.78 an hour at \$0.2227 each, and 7 of them run tasks.
1. [ ] 32
    > This counts the primary node as a worker. It manages the cluster and runs no executor.
1. [ ] 56
    > This gives each node 8 slots, two per vCPU. On our m7g nodes one vCPU is one core, and an executor gets one slot per vCPU: 4 per node.
1. [ ] 12
    > This reads "task node" as the only node type that runs tasks. Core nodes also run executors and store blocks for the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS), while task nodes run executors without storing HDFS data.

Slide: 18 (also 16)

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Spark, PySpark and Spark SQL

What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver
A notebook on an EMR cluster works with a bike-share company’s rides, stored as Parquet files on S3. Earlier cells left two DataFrames in the notebook:
per_city   Spark DataFrame    ride counts per city, built earlier from the rides files
stations   pandas DataFrame   docks per station, with each station's city

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each line, what happens when its cell runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `rides = spark.read.parquet("s3://…/bikeshare/rides/")` :: Spark records a step on the driver; no rows are read yet
    > Reading is a transformation. The driver lists the files and records the read as the first step of the plan; Spark learns the columns from one file's footer, a one-task job that reads no ride rows. The rows are scanned only when an action asks for them.
- `per_city.explain()` :: Spark records a step on the driver; no rows are read yet
    > `.explain()` makes the driver print the plan it has recorded so far, without running it: no task, no rows.
- `top = per_city.toPandas()` :: Spark sends tasks to the executors; they run now
    > `toPandas()` needs the rows of `per_city`, so the driver turns the plan into tasks and the executors read and count the rides.
- `rows = per_city.collect()` :: Spark sends tasks to the executors; they run now
    > `.collect()` asks for the rows of `per_city`, so the plan runs as tasks on the executors.
- `stations.groupby("city")["docks"].sum()` :: pandas computes on the driver; no task runs
    > `stations` is a pandas DataFrame, and pandas has no Spark plan: the sum is computed where the cell runs, and no executor gets a task.
- `top.to_csv("per_city.csv")` :: pandas computes on the driver; no task runs
    > `top` is already a pandas DataFrame, so this pandas call writes the file from the driver's Python process without starting a Spark task.
- :: pandas computes on the executors, split across them
    > A cluster does not split a pandas operation across executors. pandas runs in the driver's Python process; only a Spark action sends tasks to executors.

A delivery company keeps its fees in one 1 GB Parquet file on S3. You have a JupyterHub notebook open in your laptop’s browser; it runs on an EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge with 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB of memory each. A cell reads the file with pandas:
fees = pd.read_parquet("s3://…/delivery/fees.parquet")

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Where are the rows of `fees` held, and what is the most memory the cell can use?

1. [x] In the driver's Python process, within one node's 16 GiB
    > Every cell runs in the Spark driver. pandas works in that one Python process on one node, so the other nodes' memory does not help, and the driver's own process may be allocated less than the node's 16 GiB.
1. [ ] Across both core nodes' executors, within 32 GiB in total
    > Executors get work only from a Spark action. A pandas call is not Spark: no task is created, so the rows never leave the driver.
1. [ ] On your laptop, where the notebook is open, within its memory
    > This carries over local Jupyter, where Python runs on your laptop. On EMR the browser only sends cells and shows output: JupyterHub is on the primary node, and the cells run in the driver on a core node, so the rows of `fees` stay on the cluster.

Slide: 22, 24, 25 (also 16, 21)


What goes into the Exchange (shuffle)?
A ferry company keeps its 2025 ticket sales as one Parquet file on S3. Each row is one ticket:



sale_date
route
fare




2025-03-02
Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay
$8


2025-03-02
Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay
$10


2025-03-05
Horseshoe Bay to Nanaimo
$18


…
…
…



A PySpark query computes the average fare per route for March 2025; sales is the Spark DataFrame read from the file and F is pyspark.sql.functions:
march = sales.filter(F.col("sale_date").between("2025-03-01", "2025-03-31"))
by_route = march.groupBy("route").agg(F.avg("fare").alias("avg_fare"))
The scan stage reads the file in pieces, one piece per task, and tickets are stored in the order they were sold, so a route’s tickets are spread over several tasks. The Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay route sold 4 tickets in March, for $60 in all, so its average fare is $15. Two tasks hold those tickets:




tickets
fares
sum
average




task 1
3
$8, $10, $12
$30
$10


task 2
1
$30
$30
$30




---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## What should each task send into the `Exchange` (shuffle), so that the final stage gets \$15 from the least data?

1. [x] Its count and sum of fares for the route
    > Task 1 sends 3 and \$30, task 2 sends 1 and \$30; the final stage adds them and divides: \$60 / 4 = \$15. Each task sends two numbers per route, however many tickets it holds.
1. [ ] Its average of all its fares for the route
    > The final stage would receive two averages, \$10 from task 1 and \$30 from task 2, and could only average them: (\$10 + \$30) / 2 = \$20, not \$15. It cannot weight task 1's average by its 3 tickets, because the count did not travel. An average of averages is wrong whenever the groups differ in size.
1. [ ] Every ticket row it holds for the route
    > This also gives \$15, but every row goes into the `Exchange`. Partial totals give the same answer with two numbers per route from each task.

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Storage on the cluster

Where is each piece of data kept?
A team keeps Vancouver’s Van311 non-emergency service requests for 2025 as Parquet files on S3, and a notebook on an EMR cluster works with them:
cluster    1 primary + 2 core nodes
notebook   builds `late`, the requests that took more than 45 days to close
end        the cluster is terminated when the notebook's work ends

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Where is each of these kept? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- rows a task cannot fit in memory while it works :: the node's disk
    > When a task spills rows that do not fit in memory, it writes them to its node's disk and reads them back later.
- Spark's cache of a DataFrame once executor memory is full :: the node's disk
    > By default the cache goes into executor memory first, then onto the node's local disk; it is gone when the cluster ends.
- the rows `.collect()` returns :: driver memory
    > `.collect()` brings every row of the result into the driver's process.
- the number `late.count()` returns to the notebook :: driver memory
    > The executors count their parts; the total comes back to the driver as one Python number.
- :: S3
    > Nothing in this list is written to S3 by the cluster: these are working data that live and die with the cluster or the notebook. The inputs on S3 are not in the list.
- :: HDFS
    > HDFS pools the core nodes' disks for data that a job writes there deliberately, such as a result it will reread while the cluster runs, and it is deleted with the cluster. Shuffle files and spills use each node's local disk.

Spark: how a job runs
Driver. The program that coordinates a Spark application: it runs your code, builds the query plan and sends tasks to the executors.
Executor. A Spark program running on an EMR core or task node. It runs tasks and keeps their data in its memory or on the node’s disk.
Partition. A chunk of rows that one task processes as one unit. When reading files it holds one or more splits, each a byte range of one file, planned from the file sizes and the number of slots.
Task. One stage’s work on one chunk of rows, run in one slot: by default, one executor core.
Slot. One executor core, as room to run one task on one Spark partition at a time. An executor with 4 cores runs 4 tasks at once; our EMR nodes have one per vCPU.
Stage. A set of tasks Spark can run before rows have to move between partitions. Every task in it runs the same steps on a different partition.
Wave. The set of a stage’s tasks that run at the same time, one per slot. 36 reading tasks on 8 slots need 5 of them.
Transformation. A step such as filter or groupBy(...).count() that is only recorded in the plan. No task runs until an action asks for a result.
Action. On a Spark DataFrame, a call such as df.count(), df.collect() or df.write.parquet() that makes Spark run the plan built so far. Unlike pandas, where each step runs as soon as you call it.


Spark: shuffles and slow stages
Narrow transformation. A step each task does on its own partition, so no rows move between partitions: filter, select, withColumn.
Wide transformation. A step that needs rows from other partitions, such as groupBy, orderBy, a window or most joins. Spark adds a shuffle before it.
Shuffle (Exchange). Moving rows between partitions for the next stage: each task writes its rows to its node’s disk, and the next stage’s tasks read them, often from other nodes.
Window query. A step that computes a value over a group of rows and puts it on each row, such as each trip’s payment-type average next to the trip. Every row goes into an Exchange.
Hot key. One join, window or sort value with far more rows than the others. All its rows go to one task, which runs long after the rest of its stage; more nodes do not help.
Spill. Writing to the node’s disk when the rows a task sorts, groups or shuffles do not fit in its share of executor memory. The result is correct but slower.


EMR cluster
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node. The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node. An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node. An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing data.
HDFS. A file system that splits files into blocks across a cluster’s core nodes’ disks. Its data is lost when the cluster terminates, so our inputs and outputs stay on S3.


Also used on this page
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.

title: L4 review: scaling up, scaling out, and where the data lives
text:
Storage side of scaling up

What does each filter condition make Spark read?
A city library keeps its loan records for September to December 2025 in S3 as Parquet, one folder partition per month of loan_date:
s3://city-library/loans/
├── month=2025-09/
│   └── part-0.parquet        about 150 MB
├── month=2025-10/
│   └── part-0.parquet
├── month=2025-11/
│   └── part-0.parquet
└── month=2025-12/
    └── part-0.parquet
Each file holds only its month’s loans, in many row groups (the blocks of rows inside a Parquet file). Inside a file the rows are sorted by branch_id; the other columns, loan_date (a DATE), loan_days and patron_id, are in no particular order. Spark on an EMR cluster runs queries that each have one filter condition.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each filter condition on the loans folder, what does Spark open and read? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `month = '2025-11'` :: 1 or 2 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition names the folder key, so Spark keeps the November folder and rules out the other 3 by their names, without opening their files. Every row in the November file is a November loan, so every row matches and every row group is read.
- `month IN ('2025-11', '2025-12')` :: 1 or 2 files opened, every row group read
    > Two values of the key work the same way as one: Spark opens two folders and rules out 2 by name, then reads every row group of both files.
- `branch_id = 17` :: all 4 files opened, some row groups may be skipped
    > All 4 files are opened, because the condition does not name `month`. Inside each file the rows are sorted by branch, so each row group holds a narrow range of `branch_id`; where the writer stored each group's min and max in the footer, the reader rules out the groups whose range cannot hold 17 without fetching them.
- `loan_date = DATE '2025-11-14'` :: all 4 files opened, some row groups may be skipped
    > The `month` folders were made from the loan date, but this condition names `loan_date`, so no folder is ruled out by name and Spark opens all 4 files. Each file holds one month's loans, so every row group's min and max of `loan_date` fall inside that month: in the September, October and December files no group's range can hold 14 November 2025, so where the footer holds each group's min and max the reader skips them all. In the November file the days are in no order, so every group's range covers the day and every row group is read.
- `loan_days > 21` :: all 4 files opened, every row group read
    > The rows are not ordered by loan length, so every row group holds short and long loans and its min and max rule nothing out. Spark reads every row group of every file.
- `patron_id = 40213` :: all 4 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition matches few rows, but patron ids are spread over every row group, so each group's min and max cover 40213 and none can be ruled out.
- :: footers read, no row group read
    > A footer says where the row groups are and their min and max; it holds no rows. Spark has to read row groups to return a result.

Slide: 15, 20, 21, 23, 31


Which folder key best supports the analysts’ one-day and one-month queries?
A news site keeps its page views from January 2024 to December 2025 in S3 as one Parquet file, with no folder partitions:
s3://news-site/page-views/
└── page-views.parquet    4 GB, rows sorted by view time, many row groups
The analysts query the file with DuckDB. Their common queries filter on the view time, one day or one month, and count views per article category. The team will rewrite the file into folder partitions on one key, and the analysts will write each time filter so that it also names that key. The rewrite keeps the rows sorted by view time, with many row groups in each file. DuckDB recommends at least 100 MB per folder partition.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which folder key best supports the analysts' one-day and one-month queries?

1. [x] `month`: 24 folders of about 170 MB
    > Each query names one month, so it opens one folder. Inside that folder, the footer's minimum and maximum view times let a daily query skip other days' row groups, and each folder partition is over 100 MB.
1. [ ] `day`: 731 folders of about 5.5 MB
    > The `day` key matches the daily filter, and day folders helped the lecture's one-day query on the June file, but each 5.5 MB folder partition here is below the 100 MB guidance. A monthly query opens about 30 small folder partitions, one per day of the month, while sorting by view time already lets a daily query skip row groups within a monthly folder partition.
1. [ ] `category`: 12 folders of about 330 MB
    > The queries group by category and filter on dates. Every query needs all 12 categories, so it opens all 12 folders and the key rules nothing out.

Slide: 22–23


Which changes spread the scan over all four threads?
A hotel chain exports its 2025 bookings as one Parquet file:
bookings-2025.parquet     1.2 GB, one row group
DuckDB with four threads on an m6a.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GiB) computes the average nightly price per hotel for July 2025 in 3 s. During the query one vCPU is busy and three stay idle.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which of these changes let the July query finish sooner by spreading its scan over all four threads? Select every change that does.

- [x] Rewrite the file with many row groups
    > Row groups are the pieces a reader can split a scan into and read in parallel. With one row group the scan is a single piece, so one thread does it; DuckDB's own default write makes row groups of about 123,000 rows.
- [x] Rewrite it as folder partitions by month, one file per month
    > Two gains at once. The July query opens only July's file instead of all twelve months, and that file has many row groups, because any rewrite splits the rows into row groups, so the four threads share its scan.
- [ ] Rewrite it as folder partitions by hotel, one file per hotel
    > The threads do share the scan, one file each, but the July filter names no hotel, so every file is opened and all 1.2 GB is read for one month's rows. The key must match the filter.
- [ ] Set DuckDB to 32 threads
    > Extra threads cannot divide one row group: they have no piece to read, and the instance has only 4 vCPU to run them.
- [ ] Move to an m6a.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GiB)
    > Three vCPUs are already idle, so neither memory nor vCPUs are short. The file would still be one piece, read by one thread.

Slide: 16–19

section: Scaling out: more nodes, and a network between them
text:
Scaling out: more nodes, and a network between them

Which first change cuts the daily query’s time most?
A parcel company keeps three years of parcel scans as CSV in S3:
s3://parcel-co/scans/
├── part-0.csv
│   …
└── part-N.csv            450 GB in all, 25 columns, 2023 to 2025
A query that runs every day counts late parcels per depot for one month and reads 3 of the 25 columns. On one m6a.xlarge it takes 50 minutes, and for most of that time the instance’s network is at its limit reading from S3: the m6a.xlarge’s baseline is 1.56 Gbps, about 195 MB/s, so reading all 450 GB takes about 38 minutes.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which first change is likely to cut the daily query's time most?

1. [x] Convert the CSV once to Parquet
    > The query then fetches 3 of the 25 columns, compressed and stored as typed values, so most of the 450 GB never crosses the network. L1's taxi query went from 14 min to 5.5 s this way on one instance.
1. [ ] Run the query on EMR with three core nodes
    > Three nodes bring about three times the network, so at best about a third of the time, and together they still read every byte of the CSV.
1. [ ] Split the CSV into many smaller files
    > Smaller files cut the same 450 GB into more pieces, and every piece still crosses the same network.

Slide: 3, 24, 30


Which node type should the team add for this job?
An EMR cluster with one primary node and two core nodes runs a long Spark job that reads its input from S3 and writes its results back to S3. To make the job finish sooner, the team that runs it wants to add nodes for this job and remove them afterwards without losing any data the cluster stores.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which node type should the team add for this job?

1. [x] Task nodes
    > Task nodes do work and store none of the cluster's distributed data, so removing them later loses nothing; the input and the results stay in S3.
1. [ ] Core nodes
    > Core nodes also do work, but they store the cluster's distributed data on their disks, so removing one later takes its share of that data with it.
1. [ ] Larger primary node
    > The primary node manages the cluster and coordinates its services. The job runs on the core and task nodes, so enlarging the primary does not add processing capacity to those nodes.

Slide: 29


After how many queries has the rewrite paid back?
Vancouver publishes its Van311 non-emergency service requests as open data. A team keeps five years of them in S3 as one CSV file per year, and a weekly query reads them all:
s3://van-311/requests/
├── 2021.csv
│   …
└── 2025.csv
Rewriting the CSV files once as sorted Parquet in folder partitions uses 1,200 CPU-seconds. The weekly query uses 50 CPU-seconds on the CSV and 10 CPU-seconds on the rewritten files.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## After how many weekly queries has the rewrite paid back its CPU-seconds?

1. [x] 30 queries
    > Each query saves 50 − 10 = 40 CPU-seconds, and 1,200 / 40 = 30 weekly runs.
1. [ ] 24 queries
    > 1,200 / 50 divides by what the old query cost. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 40 CPU-seconds.
1. [ ] 120 queries
    > 1,200 / 10 divides by what the new query costs. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 40 CPU-seconds.
1. [ ] 20 queries
    > 1,200 / (50 + 10) adds the two costs together. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 50 − 10 = 40 CPU-seconds.

Slide: 32

title: L4 review: scaling up, scaling out, and where the data lives
section: Case (A2): Best model search for the taxi data
text:
Case (A2): Best model search for the taxi data

Scale up, scale out, or neither?
Each workload below runs today on one EC2 instance, an m6a.large (2 vCPU, 8 GiB of RAM), unless the row says otherwise. The lecture named these moves for a workload on one instance:
scale up    replace the instance with a larger one (more vCPUs, RAM and network on one instance)
scale out   run the work on a cluster of several nodes
neither     keep the one instance as it is

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which scaling move does each workload need? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A team of 3 shares a Jupyter environment on the m6a.large and now needs 64 GiB of RAM for a 24 GB dataset :: Scale up
    > One larger EC2 instance gives the team the RAM, and the data fits on one instance.
- Training 100 random forest models with different hyperparameters on a 6 GB dataset takes 12 hours on the largest instance you can get, and the results are needed in 3 hours :: Scale out
    > The models are independent, so they can run on several nodes at once. Because no larger instance is available, four equivalent nodes (12 hours / 3 hours) with ideal scaling reduce the 12-hour run to about 3 hours.
- A dashboard queries a 500 MB SQLite database on the m6a.large :: Neither
    > 500 MB fits in memory on a small instance, and nothing else in the task asks for more.
- A weekly report on an m6a.xlarge (16 GiB of RAM) reads 2 of 40 columns from a 7 GB Parquet file and finishes in 20 seconds :: Neither
    > The reader fetches only the 2 columns it needs, and the report already finishes in seconds, so there is nothing for a larger instance or a cluster to fix.
- Processing 2 PB of genomic sequencing data from 200 research institutions, which the m6a.large would read through one network link :: Scale out
    > One instance reads all 2 PB through one network and works on it with one instance's vCPUs, and even the largest instance is a ceiling. A cluster reads and works on parts of the data on every node at once.
- The m6a.large's 8 GiB of RAM cannot hold a 15 GB Parquet file that a training step needs in memory all at once :: Scale up
    > One larger instance holds the data in memory, and no cluster is needed. The file is compressed, so the loaded data takes more than 15 GB: pick an instance with well over 15 GB of RAM.
- :: Larger EBS volume
    > None of these workloads is short of disk space. A volume stores files; it adds no RAM, vCPUs or network.

Which shape of demand is this?

## A university's course-registration site gets almost no traffic for weeks. When registration opens at 8:00 one morning, about 20,000 students load its pages within ten minutes, and the traffic is back to almost nothing by noon. Which time shape of demand is this?

1. [x] Burst
    > Nothing for weeks, then nearly all the load within minutes: what must be bought is capacity for those ten minutes.
1. [ ] Daily rhythm
    > A daily rhythm repeats every day, busy at midday and near zero overnight. This peak comes on one morning, with weeks of near silence around it.
1. [ ] Scheduled job
    > A clock sets when the students arrive, but the load is thousands of separate requests from people. A scheduled job is one run started by a clock, with nothing between runs.

title: L4 review: scaling up, scaling out, and where the data lives
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise them in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Parquet
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Row group. A horizontal block inside one Parquet file, holding one column chunk per column. Its size is set when the file is written, and a file can hold one or many.
Column chunk. The values of one field within one row group of a Parquet file. The writer can store their min and max, which lets a reader skip the whole row group.
Footer. The metadata at the end of a Parquet file: the schema, where each column chunk starts and, if the writer stored them, each chunk’s min and max. A reader fetches it before any data.
Projection pushdown. Handing the reader the list of columns a query uses, so it reads only those columns from a Parquet file.
Predicate pushdown. Handing the reader the query’s filter, so it can skip row groups whose stored min and max show that no row can match.


Layout and files on S3
Folder partition. A dataset layout with one named location per value of a column, such as day=2012-06-14/ (on S3, a prefix). A filter on that column skips the other locations without opening them.
Compaction. Rewriting many small files into fewer, larger ones, so a query opens fewer files. Too few files, or too few row groups, can leave cores idle.
Prefix. The leading part of an object’s name, such as day=2012-06-14/. S3 lists objects by it, and the console’s folders are built from it; the general-purpose buckets we use have no real folders.
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.
Byte-range read. Asking S3 for one stated part of an object instead of the whole object. Parquet libraries fetch the footer this way, then only the column chunks a query needs.


Memory and resources
Eager load. Reading the whole dataset into memory before the work starts. If data and working space exceed memory, the operating system swaps to disk or stops the program.
Storage, memory, compute and network. The four things every data task uses, each with a capacity and a rate. Looking at a job from each in turn helps find its bottleneck, and cloud architecture often trades one for another.
EBS volume. A disk an EC2 instance reaches over the network, as its main disk or an extra one. Its data survives a stop, and it bills per GB-month while it exists, even when the instance is stopped.


Also used on this page
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
Time shape of demand. When a workload asks for its resources across a day or a week: a steady rate, a daily rhythm, a burst, or a scheduled job. With the peak rate, it decides whether provisioned or usage-based billing is cheaper.
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node (EMR). The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node (EMR). An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node (EMR). An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing data.

title: Midterm review
text:
Block 1: lectures 1 to 3

1. Whose job is it, from AWS’s side

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## In which service is each of these **AWS's** responsibility, not yours? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The hardware: the racks and the power :: Both
    > The provider's floor is the same whatever you rent above it.
- The virtual machine layer the code runs on :: Both
    > An instance is a virtual machine on AWS's hardware, and a function runs in a small virtual machine AWS starts for it. Either way AWS operates that layer.
- Patching the operating system :: Lambda
    > On a function the operating system moved to AWS's side with the runtime and the capacity. On an instance it is yours from the first boot.
- Patching the language runtime the code uses :: Lambda
    > You pick a runtime version from AWS's list and AWS patches it. On an instance you install the runtime, so patching it is yours.
- The code that does the work :: Neither
    > The provider never writes it, whichever way you run it.
- The policy that says what your code may touch :: Neither
    > A role on an instance, an execution role on a function. AWS enforces the policy on both and writes it on neither.
- :: EC2
    > Nothing AWS runs for you on an instance is missing on a function. On EC2 it runs the bottom two bands; on Lambda those two and three more.



2. Stop or terminate

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## An EC2 instance was launched with its own volume, left on the default of being deleted when the instance is terminated. A second volume was attached later to hold the data, and that one was set to be kept when the instance is terminated. Each volume is billed for the space it takes while it exists. Which condition does each description below fit? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Both volumes are there, and the per-second compute charge is being paid :: Running instance
    > Nothing has been switched off, so the machine bills and both volumes bill.
- Both volumes are there and billing, and no compute charge is being paid :: Stopped instance
    > Stopping pauses the machine and leaves the storage alone. The storage is what carries on costing.
- The launch volume and everything installed on it are kept for the next start, and the compute bill has stopped :: Stopped instance
    > You pay for the storage over the weekend so that Monday starts where Friday ended.
- The launch volume is gone, and the volume attached later is billing on its own :: Terminated instance
    > The launch volume was set to delete. The attached volume was set to be kept, so it outlives the instance and bills with nothing to show for it.
- The launch volume no longer exists, and neither does what was installed on it :: Terminated instance
    > The launch volume was left on its default, so terminating the instance deleted it along with everything on it.
- Somebody is logged in right now, and the compute bill is growing by the second :: Running instance
    > Billing by the second happens while it runs, whether or not anyone is using it.
- :: Instance never launched
    > Every description here is of a machine that exists and has volumes attached to it.



3. Launch settings for a notebook instance

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## You launch one EC2 instance to explore a dataset in a Jupyter notebook. The data is 10 GB in a compressed Parquet file in S3. Which launch setting settles each requirement below? Not all options will be used.

- Python 3.12 and the AWS CLI must already be in place the first time the machine boots: no install commands may run at all, not even at first boot :: Image
    > The image is what the machine starts from: its operating system and the software already on it. A user data script could install Python at first boot, but the requirement rules out running any install commands.
- Loaded into pandas, the file takes about 30 GB of memory, and the whole DataFrame must fit in memory at once :: Instance type
    > The type fixes memory, cores and network. Disk space doesn't help: a DataFrame is held in memory, and the file itself stays in S3.
- AWS lets connections reach the machine only on port 8888, and only from your own IP address :: Security group
    > It decides which ports are reachable from which addresses. It does not check who you are, or decide what the machine may read in S3.
- The notebook reads the file from S3 without anyone putting access keys in a file on the machine :: Role
    > An EC2 instance can be given a role. Its policy says what the instance may read, so no one has to paste access keys into a file on the machine.
- :: User data script
    > Commands the machine runs at first boot. Here everything needed is either in the image or set by another setting.
- :: Volume size
    > It sets disk space, not memory, and the file is read from S3, not stored on the disk.



4. A function or an instance

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which fits each piece of work best? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A file of a few MB lands in an S3 bucket a few times an hour and needs a few seconds of work to convert :: A function
    > Short, started by an event, and idle most of the hour. No compute runs or is paid for between arrivals.
- A model fit on a 2 GB table that takes forty minutes, cannot be broken into shorter steps, and runs once a night :: An EC2 instance
    > One call of a function stops at fifteen minutes, and this job cannot be split into calls that fit. A machine started for the job and stopped after it is the shape left, and the table fits in its memory.
- Someone working in a notebook all afternoon on a 5 GB table, changing code and re-running it :: An EC2 instance
    > The session has to stay up between keystrokes, and the data in memory has to survive from one cell to the next. Saving files between calls moves the files, not the session.
- A web endpoint answering a few short requests a minute, at all hours, where a second's delay now and then is fine :: A function
    > Almost always idle, and each request is short. The bill follows the requests, not the hours.
- A daily summary of yesterday's 200 MB that takes two minutes and writes one file :: A function
    > Short, scheduled and rare. A machine kept for it would sit idle for the rest of the day.
- :: A cluster of several machines
    > Every workload here fits on one machine, in its memory and in its time. Spreading work over several machines pays only when one cannot do it.



5. What starts the function

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A smart-home company runs several functions. What starts the function in each situation below? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Someone asks the voice assistant "what is the temperature?" and it answers a second later :: Request
    > Someone is waiting for the reply: a request starts the function and gets the answer back.
- A thermostat writes a new reading file to a bucket, and a function checks whether it is outside the safe range :: Event
    > The new file is the event; its arrival starts the function. Nobody waits for the check.
- A new firmware file is uploaded to a bucket, and a function checks its signature :: Event
    > The upload is the event; a rule sends it to the function. Nobody waits for the result.
- A new recording from a door camera lands in a bucket, and a function blurs the faces in it :: Event
    > The recording's arrival is the event; a rule sends it to the function. Nobody waits for the result.
- Every night at 03:00 a function deletes test devices' logs older than a week :: Schedule
    > A clock starts it.
- On the first day of each month a function totals each household's energy use :: Schedule
    > A fixed date on the calendar: a schedule.
- :: Deployment
    > Deploying a new version puts the code in place. It does not run until a request, an event or a schedule starts it.



6. Why the Parquet read is small

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A city keeps three years of bike-share rides in S3 as Parquet, already compressed, 4.2 GB, sorted by start time, in 60 row groups. A query asks for the average ride duration per station in March 2025, which needs one month and 3 of the file's 14 columns. Run with DuckDB against the Parquet copy, it reads 35 MB from S3. What explains the reduction from 4.2 GB to 35 MB?

1. [x] The 11 unneeded columns are never fetched, and the footer's statistics rule out row groups that cannot match
    > Two savings at once. Each column's bytes are stored apart, so the 11 unneeded columns are never read, and the minimum and maximum start time per row group rule out every group outside March 2025.
1. [ ] S3 applies the filter inside the bucket and returns only the rows that match
    > In this DuckDB run, S3 returns the requested byte ranges; it does not run the query. The reader reads the footer, decides which byte ranges it needs, and asks for those.
1. [ ] The data is compressed on the way across the network, so far fewer bytes have to travel
    > The 4.2 GB is already the compressed size. The reduction comes from not reading most of the file at all.
1. [ ] The whole file is fetched and the unwanted parts are dropped once it arrives
    > That would move all 4.2 GB. The reader fetches the footer first, which says where each column and row group sits and the minimum and maximum in each, then asks only for the byte ranges it needs.



7. Where the S3 client is made

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A Lambda function, with default settings, has the line `s3 = boto3.client("s3")` as the first line of its handler, then uses the client to write one small file. A hundred calls arrive in a minute, one after another, and one execution environment serves them all. Which statement is true?

1. [x] The client is created on every call
    > Everything inside the handler runs on every call. Code at module level runs once, when the environment starts, and the calls after that reuse what it made.
1. [ ] The client is created once, because Lambda keeps objects made inside the handler between calls
    > A local made in the handler is gone when the call returns; only what module level made is there for the next call.
1. [ ] The client is created once, when the code is deployed
    > Deploying puts the code in place. None of it runs until an environment starts to serve a call.
1. [ ] The client is created once, when the environment starts, as if the line were at module level
    > The line is inside the handler, so it runs when the handler runs: on every call. Only code outside the handler runs when the environment starts.

## Which way of running it fits each piece of work best? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A mobile app asks, a few times a minute, for the nearest open store; each answer takes 200 ms to compute :: A Lambda function
    > A short answer to a request, with nothing to keep running between requests.
- Every hour an EventBridge schedule starts a check that a website answers, which takes a second :: A Lambda function
    > A short task on a schedule, with nothing to keep running between checks.
- A model is trained on a 3 GB table for two hours in one Python process, after which the machine is not needed :: One EC2 instance
    > One process on one machine, far longer than a function may run, and nothing to stop afterwards but the instance.
- A FastAPI app on port 8000 loads a 2 GB table when it starts and answers `/summary` requests all day :: One EC2 instance
    > A process that stays up and holds state; one machine holds 2 GB.
- A Spark job on 3 TB needs a node type with a lot of memory that the team picks itself :: An EMR cluster you start and stop
    > Too big for one machine, and the team wants to choose the nodes' instance type, which an EMR cluster lets it do.
- Ten analysts share Spark notebooks on one cluster all week, with node types the team chose :: An EMR cluster you start and stop
    > A cluster kept up for many notebooks, on nodes the team picked: EMR on EC2.
- :: An AWS Glue job
    > On Glue the workers last for one job and nobody picks machines. Every Spark row here needs chosen node types or a cluster that stays up all week.

## A scooter-share company keeps its trips as Parquet in S3, in one folder for each trip date: `trip_date=2025-07-01/`, `trip_date=2025-07-02/`, and so on. Each folder holds one file, sorted by scooter id, with about 10 row groups. Each row group's footer records the minimum and maximum of each column, and Spark can use them. Which data can Spark skip for each condition? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-14' AND scooter_id = 'SC-0417'` :: Whole folders and row groups
    > The date names one folder, so the others are skipped. Inside that day's file, sorted by scooter id, the footers rule out the row groups that cannot hold SC-0417.
- `WHERE trip_date IN ('2025-07-14', '2025-07-15')` :: Whole folders
    > Two folders match by name, and all the others are skipped. Inside them every row is needed.
- `WHERE scooter_id BETWEEN 'SC-0400' AND 'SC-0499'` :: Only row groups inside the files
    > The condition does not name the folder column, so every day's folder is opened. Each file is sorted by scooter id, so the footers rule out the row groups outside that range.
- `WHERE scooter_id = 'SC-0417' AND battery_end < 10`. Every row group has some trips that ended below 10% battery :: Only row groups inside the files
    > The scooter id rules out row groups in every file. The battery condition rules out nothing.
- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-14' AND battery_end < 10`. Every row group has some trips that ended below 10% battery :: Whole folders
    > The date skips the other folders. Inside that day's file the battery condition rules out no row group.
- `WHERE battery_end < 10 AND city = 'Vancouver'`. Every row group has trips from every city, some below 10% battery :: Neither folders nor row groups
    > Neither column names the folders, and every row group holds both kinds of trip.
- :: In S3, the rows that do not match
    > S3 hands back the byte ranges Spark asks for. Spark decides what to skip, from folder names and footers.

## In a PySpark notebook on an EMR cluster, `recent` is a Spark DataFrame of 2025's ticket sales made from Parquet files in S3, `pd` is pandas, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`. What happens when each line runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `venues_pd = pd.read_parquet("s3://tickets-raw/venues.parquet")` :: pandas does the work in the driver only, with no Spark plan
    > This is pandas: it runs in the driver's process alone.
- `large_pd = venues_pd[venues_pd["seats"] > 1000]` :: pandas does the work in the driver only, with no Spark plan
    > This is pandas filtering in the driver: no Spark plan, no tasks.
- `avg_seats = venues_pd["seats"].mean()` :: pandas does the work in the driver only, with no Spark plan
    > Still pandas on the driver: no plan, no tasks.
- `by_price = recent.orderBy(F.col("price").desc())` :: Spark adds a step to the plan. No task starts
    > A sort is a transformation too: it goes into the plan and waits for an action.
- `n = recent.count()` :: Tasks start on the executors
    > Counting is an action: the plan runs and the number comes back to the driver.
- `recent_pd = recent.toPandas()` :: Tasks start on the executors
    > toPandas is an action: tasks read and filter on the executors, then every row is sent to the driver.
- :: S3 filters the rows before they come to Spark
    > S3 returns the bytes it is asked for. Filters run in Spark's tasks, or in pandas on the driver.

## A PySpark notebook on an EMR cluster reads a month of parcel scans, stored as 30 daily Parquet files, and writes each depot's totals as Parquet. The cluster is terminated at the end of the day. Where is each thing below kept while the notebook runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The 300 depot totals, turned into a pandas DataFrame with toPandas() to draw a chart in the notebook :: In the memory of the driver
    > toPandas() brings the rows back from the executors into one pandas DataFrame, in the driver's process.
- A small list of depot names read with pd.read_csv in the notebook :: In the memory of the driver
    > This is pandas, not Spark: it runs in the driver alone and keeps its DataFrame there.
- Files an earlier job saved on the cluster's HDFS for a later job on the same cluster :: On the disk of a node
    > HDFS keeps its blocks on the core nodes' disks, and they go when the cluster does.
- A temporary file a task creates in its node's local folder and deletes before the task ends :: On the disk of a node
    > A task's own scratch file sits on the node that runs it.
- A public Parquet dataset that several teams' clusters read :: In an S3 bucket
    > Shared by many clusters and kept after each one ends: S3.
- A results file a teammate opens next week, after this cluster is terminated :: In an S3 bucket
    > The cluster's disks go with it, so anything needed later goes to S3.
- :: In the Glue Data Catalog
    > The catalog keeps table definitions, the metadata, not the rows. None of these is a table definition.

## To save money, a cluster shrinks from 2 core nodes to 1, so from 8 slots to 4. In one scan stage, 12 tasks read rows, and each takes about the same time. A task starts when a slot is free, and nothing else changes. How does the stage's time change?

1. [x] It grows to about one and a half times the old time
    > On 8 slots, 12 tasks run in two waves: 8, then 4. On 4 slots they run in three waves of 4.
1. [ ] It grows to about twice the old time
    > Half the slots does not mean twice the waves. Count them: two before, three after.
1. [ ] It grows to about three times the old time
    > Three is the number of waves on 4 slots, not how much longer the stage takes. Before, it took two.
1. [ ] It stays about the same
    > With 4 slots, 4 of the 12 tasks now wait for a free slot, so a third wave is added.

---

## A 230 MB Parquet file holds 6 row groups of about the same size. The cluster grows from 8 slots to 16, and Spark's scan of the file now makes 16 tasks. How many of those tasks read rows?

1. [x] 6: only the ranges that hold a row group's middle read rows
    > Spark cuts the file into about 16 byte ranges. Spark never divides a row group between ranges; one range reads each of the 6 row groups.
1. [ ] 16: each task reads half of a row group
    > A row group is never split between tasks. The task whose range holds its middle reads all of it.
1. [ ] 1: only the first task reads rows
    > That is what a file with one row group does. Here there are 6 middles, spread across the file.
1. [ ] 16: each range reads every row group it overlaps
    > A row group goes to one range only, the one that holds its middle, so nothing is read twice.

## A mapping company must render 2,400 satellite image tiles on an EMR cluster before the morning. The tiles are independent of each other, and each takes 5 minutes on one vCPU. They can be spread over any number of vCPUs with no overhead. The cluster has one primary node, which renders nothing, plus core nodes of type m6a.xlarge, each with 4 vCPUs for rendering. Launch takes 10 minutes before the first tile can start, and everything must finish 4 hours after the cluster starts, launch included. Step 1: how much work is it, in vCPU-hours?

1. [x] 200
    > 2,400 tiles × 5 minutes is 12,000 vCPU-minutes, which is 200 vCPU-hours.
1. [ ] 12,000
    > That is the work in vCPU-minutes. Divided by 60 it is 200 vCPU-hours.
1. [ ] 2,400
    > That is the number of tiles. Each one is 5 minutes of one vCPU's work.
1. [ ] 50
    > That divides by the 4 vCPUs of a node, which gives node-hours, not the work itself.

## Step 2: what is the smallest number of core nodes that finishes in time?

1. [x] 14
    > After the 10-minute launch, 3 hours 50 minutes are left. 200 vCPU-hours over about 3.83 hours needs about 52.2 vCPUs at once: 53, which is 13.25 nodes, so 14.
1. [ ] 13
    > Thirteen nodes give 52 vCPUs, and 200 vCPU-hours over 52 vCPUs takes about 3 hours 51 minutes: just over the 3 hours 50 minutes left once the 10-minute launch is taken out.
1. [ ] 15
    > Fourteen nodes already give 56 vCPUs, more than the 53 needed.
1. [ ] 50
    > 200 vCPU-hours divided by 4 vCPUs per node is a number of node-hours, not of nodes. It still has to be spread over the hours left.

## A delivery company keeps three years of parcel scans in S3 as Parquet, about 200 GB a year. Each row is one scan: the scan time, the depot (300 depots), the parcel id (80 million parcels) and the status. Each week an audit job reads all three years of scans at one depot, a different depot each week. Which folder key lets that job skip all the other data, while keeping the number of folders small and each folder large?

1. [x] Depot
    > The job reads one depot's folder and skips the other 299. Three years over 300 depots is about 2 GB a folder.
1. [ ] Scan date
    > Every date folder holds scans from every depot, so the job would have to open all of them.
1. [ ] Scan hour
    > The same problem as the date, and about 26,000 small folders on top of it.
1. [ ] Parcel id
    > 80 million folders of a few rows each, and nothing in the name says which depot a parcel passed through.

## After an Exchange by store, a stage runs 200 tasks. The median task takes 0.3 seconds on about 50 thousand rows; one task takes 40 seconds on 9 million rows. What is the most likely cause of the slow stage?

1. [x] One key has many more rows than the others
    > Every row with the same key goes to the same task after the Exchange, so a store with far more rows than the others lands all of them on one task.
1. [ ] The rows each task holds do not fit in the memory available to that task
    > Memory per task is the same for all 200 tasks. One task forty times the median points to what that task holds, not to how much memory each task has.
1. [ ] Too few readable parts of the input
    > That shows up in a scan stage, as tasks that read no rows. This stage comes after an Exchange.
1. [ ] Too many small files and folders
    > Small files slow down listing and the start of a scan. They do not make one task after an Exchange forty times the others.

## A team moves a nightly PySpark job from an AWS Glue job to an EMR cluster on EC2. On EMR, what does the team now choose that it did not choose on Glue?

1. [x] The EC2 instance type of each node
    > On EMR the team rents nodes and picks their instance types. On Glue there were no machines to pick.
1. [ ] The Spark version the job runs on
    > Both fix it: the EMR release on EMR, the Glue version on Glue.
1. [ ] The PySpark code of the job
    > The team writes the code on both. Only where it runs changes.
1. [ ] The S3 bucket the job reads from
    > The team names its input on both. What changes is what the team rents to run the job.
